subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 38-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus eats a large high-carbohydrate meal. Within 2 hours her hepatic malonyl-CoA level rises several-fold and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation falls.
question: Which of the following best explains the decrease in hepatic fatty acid oxidation?

options.text: Inhibition of beta-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase by NADH
Malonyl-CoA inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I

explanation_correct: In the fed state, insulin and citrate activate acetyl-CoA carboxylase, raising malonyl-CoA. Malonyl-CoA inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, the rate-limiting step for entry of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria, so fatty acid synthesis and fatty acid oxidation are reciprocally regulated.

explanation_incorrect.A: Carnitine availability does not fall after a meal; the shuttle is regulated by malonyl-CoA inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I.
explanation_incorrect.B: NADH is a product of the third reaction of beta-oxidation and does not inhibit beta-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase, which is inhibited by its product acetyl-CoA.
explanation_incorrect.D: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity is not the acute regulatory step in this setting.
explanation_incorrect.E: Increased mitochondrial acetyl-CoA does not block beta-oxidation; it activates pyruvate carboxylase for gluconeogenesis.

educationalObjective: Malonyl-CoA produced by acetyl-CoA carboxylase inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I and suppresses mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation.
